hypotheses.title: LSASS Handle with Credential-Access Memory Mask
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor with elevated access on Windows is suspected of reading lsass.exe process memory to extract authentication material. Hunt for non-system processes opening handles to lsass.exe with credential-access or all-access masks, particularly when CallTrace includes UNKNOWN or unexpected DLLs indicating direct syscall or manual API use.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 10
pivots.detail: TargetImage = lsass.exe AND GrantedAccess IN (0x1010, 0x1038, 0x1400, 0x1410, 0x1438, 0x143a, 0x1fffff, 0x1f0fff) AND SourceImage NOT IN (WerFault.exe, WerFaultSecure.exe, Sysmon64.exe, MsMpEng.exe, csrss.exe)

pivots.label: CallTrace anomaly
pivots.detail: CallTrace containing UNKNOWN = direct syscall (NanoDump, custom loaders). CallTrace ending in dbgcore.dll or dbghelp.dll = debugging API path used by ProcDump and older Mimikatz. Modern Mimikatz routes through ntdll.dll alone.

pivots.label: Timing & frequency
pivots.detail: LSASS access >30 min after the last user logon, from a process with no prior LSASS access history, or clustered with 5+ unique source processes within 10 minutes — all significantly raise confidence.

hypotheses.fpr: AV/EDR products, WerFault.exe, Sysmon itself, and tools such as Process Explorer all legitimately access LSASS. Exclude by signed binary + known install path. Alert only when SourceImage is not in an org-maintained allowlist.

hypotheses.title: comsvcs.dll MiniDump Abuse via rundll32
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of abusing the comsvcs.dll MiniDumpW export via rundll32.exe to dump LSASS memory without deploying external tools. Hunt for rundll32.exe command lines combining comsvcs with MiniDump or ordinal references alongside a PID or the string lsass.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1
pivots.detail: Image = rundll32.exe AND CommandLine contains (comsvcs.dll OR comsvcs) AND CommandLine contains (MiniDump OR #24 OR #65560 OR full)

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 10
pivots.detail: TargetImage = lsass.exe AND CallTrace contains comsvcs.dll AND GrantedAccess = 0x1fffff. Correlate with an EID 1 for rundll32 within 2 seconds of the access event.

pivots.label: PowerShell variant
pivots.detail: Also hunt EID 4104 ScriptBlockText contains 'MiniDump' AND 'comsvcs'.

hypotheses.fpr: No legitimate administrative use case invokes comsvcs.dll MiniDump against lsass.exe. Near-zero FPR. Confirm by checking for output .dmp file creation within seconds of the rundll32 event.

hypotheses.title: SysInternals ProcDump Targeting LSASS
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using SysInternals ProcDump to write a full LSASS memory dump to disk for offline credential extraction. Hunt for procdump.exe or procdump64.exe process creation with command-line arguments naming lsass by name or PID, especially when executed from non-standard paths or unusual parent processes.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1
pivots.detail: Image endswith (procdump.exe OR procdump64.exe) AND (CommandLine contains '-ma lsass' OR CommandLine contains '-mm lsass' OR CommandLine contains lsass.exe)

pivots.label: Parent process
pivots.detail: ProcDump launched from cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wmiexec, or psexec parent is highly suspicious. Execution from a UNC path indicates remote tool staging.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 11
pivots.detail: File created by procdump.exe with .dmp extension in a temp or user-writable directory within seconds of process creation confirms a successful dump.

hypotheses.fpr: ProcDump is a legitimate SysInternals tool. Allowlist execution from C:\Program Files when the target is not lsass and the parent is a recognized IDE or support session. Alert on: lsass target, unusual parent, staging path, off-hours.

hypotheses.title: LSASS Dump File Creation in Staging Path
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of having successfully dumped LSASS memory to a file in a staging path for subsequent exfiltration. Hunt for .dmp files created in world-writable or temp directories by any process with prior LSASS handle activity, or by Task Manager as a low-tech operator dump technique.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 11
pivots.detail: TargetFilename endswith .dmp AND (TargetFilename contains lsass OR Image endswith taskmgr.exe OR Image endswith procdump.exe OR Image endswith rundll32.exe) AND path matches (%TEMP%\* OR C:\Windows\Temp\* OR C:\ProgramData\*)

pivots.label: File size heuristic
pivots.detail: LSASS memory dumps are typically 30–150 MB. A large .dmp file in %TEMP% or AppData created outside a crash scenario is a strong indicator — correlate file size with creation process.

pivots.label: Task Manager variant
pivots.detail: Image = taskmgr.exe AND TargetFilename contains lsass AND TargetFilename endswith .dmp — covers the low-tech manual dump technique documented in PYSA/Mespinoza campaigns.

refs.label: DFIR Report — PYSA Task Manager dumps

hypotheses.fpr: WerFault.exe and WerFaultSecure.exe legitimately create LSASS-related crash dumps — exclude those processes. Developer crash dump sessions may produce .dmp files in custom paths; correlate with active debugging sessions.

hypotheses.title: Encoded PowerShell with Execution-Policy Bypass Flags
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using encoded PowerShell commands combined with execution-policy bypass flags to conceal payload content and evade inspection. Hunt for powershell.exe spawned with -enc or -EncodedCommand alongside -NoP, -NonI, -W Hidden, or -Exec Bypass.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1
pivots.detail: Image endswith powershell.exe AND CommandLine contains (-enc OR -EncodedCommand) AND CommandLine contains (-nop OR -NonInteractive OR hidden OR bypass)

pivots.label: Decode and inspect
pivots.detail: Decode the -enc argument (Base64). If the plaintext contains IEX, DownloadString, Invoke-*, reflection patterns, or AmsiUtils — escalate immediately.

pivots.label: String length heuristic
pivots.detail: Legitimate admin encoded commands are typically <500 characters. Payloads >1,500 characters post-Base64 often represent multi-layer compressed or obfuscated payloads.

hypotheses.fpr: SCCM, Intune, and GPO delivery scripts often use encoding for safe transport. Allowlist by signed binary, scheduled task context, execution from C:\Windows\System32 or C:\Program Files, and known admin workstations.

hypotheses.title: In-Memory Download Cradle (Fileless Execution)
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using a PowerShell download cradle — Net.WebClient.DownloadString or Invoke-WebRequest piped into IEX — to fetch and execute a remote payload entirely in memory. Hunt for ScriptBlock log events containing both a web-client download method and an invocation expression within the same or consecutive events.

pivots.label: PS EID 4104 — primary
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (DownloadString OR DownloadData OR WebClient) AND ScriptBlockText contains (IEX OR Invoke-Expression OR &([scriptblock]::Create))

pivots.label: Network correlation
pivots.detail: Correlate EID 4104 match with Sysmon EID 3 from powershell.exe to the same destination within ±5 seconds. Non-browser PS network connections to external IPs or newly-registered domains warrant automatic escalation.

pivots.label: Obfuscated variant
pivots.detail: Attackers split 'DownloadString' across variables or use character arrays. Hunt for Net.WebClient in ScriptBlock text as a stable anchor and flag any block followed within 5 seconds by a second high-entropy ScriptBlock.

refs.label: DFIR Report — Cobalt Strike staging chains
Elastic: execution via PowerShell download cradle

hypotheses.fpr: Legitimate admin scripts use Invoke-WebRequest to pull resources from known CDNs or internal update servers. Allowlist by destination domain: Microsoft, GitHub, corporate infrastructure. Alert on unknown or new destination domains.

hypotheses.title: AMSI Bypass via PowerShell Reflection
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of patching the AMSI scan interface in memory using .NET reflection to disable antimalware scanning before executing a concealed payload. Hunt for ScriptBlock log events containing AmsiUtils, amsiInitFailed, or reflection-based SetValue calls targeting System.Management.Automation assemblies.

pivots.label: PS EID 4104 — direct
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (AmsiUtils OR amsiInitFailed) OR (ScriptBlockText contains System.Management.Automation AND SetValue AND amsi)

pivots.label: PS EID 4104 — obfuscated
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains [Ref].Assembly.GetType AND System.Management.Automation AND SetValue. Also hunt character-array construction of 'AmsiUtils' via [cHAr] concatenation or -replace/-join patterns.

pivots.label: Behavioral follow-up
pivots.detail: AMSI bypass is almost always followed within seconds by a second ScriptBlock executing the concealed payload. A gap <5 seconds between AmsiUtils ScriptBlock and a high-entropy second block = confirmed evasion chain.

hypotheses.fpr: In production environments outside approved red team windows, legitimate AMSI bypass activity is essentially zero. Alert on any occurrence and investigate promptly.

hypotheses.title: Offensive Framework Cmdlets via ScriptBlock Logging
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of executing PowerShell-based offensive framework modules from PowerSploit, PowerView, Empire, or Mimikatz captured in ScriptBlock logs. Hunt for EID 4104 events containing known offensive cmdlet names across credential dumping, lateral movement, AD enumeration, and defense evasion categories.

pivots.label: Credential dumping
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (Invoke-Mimikatz OR Invoke-NinjaCopy OR Get-GPPPassword OR Invoke-Kerberoast OR Invoke-DCSync OR Out-Minidump)

pivots.label: Lateral movement
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (Invoke-PsExec OR Invoke-WMICommand OR Invoke-SMBExec OR Invoke-TheHash OR Enter-PSSession)

pivots.label: Discovery & enumeration
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (Invoke-BloodHound OR Get-DomainAdmin OR Find-DomainShares OR Invoke-UserHunter OR Get-NetComputer OR Get-NetUser)

pivots.label: Defense evasion
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (Set-MpPreference -Disable* OR Remove-MpPreference OR Invoke-BypassUAC OR Invoke-TokenManipulation OR Add-Persistence)

refs.label: CISA AA25-141A — Akira PS credential dumping

hypotheses.fpr: The listed cmdlets are exclusively offensive with no legitimate administrative use. FPR is near-zero; any match warrants immediate investigation. EID 4104 requires ScriptBlock logging enabled via GPO.

hypotheses.title: Classic Remote Thread Injection into Legitimate Process
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of injecting malicious code into a legitimate host process using VirtualAllocEx / WriteProcessMemory / CreateRemoteThread to achieve execution under a trusted identity. Hunt for Sysmon EID 8 (CreateRemoteThread) where the source process is unexpected and the target is a common host such as explorer.exe, svchost.exe, or notepad.exe.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 8
pivots.detail: SourceImage NOT IN (known EDR/AV binaries) AND TargetImage IN (explorer.exe, svchost.exe, lsass.exe, notepad.exe, rundll32.exe, dllhost.exe) AND StartAddress NOT startswith TargetImage module base

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 10 correlation
pivots.detail: SourceImage opens handle to TargetImage with GrantedAccess = 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) or 0x43a (PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD + PROCESS_VM_WRITE + PROCESS_VM_OPERATION + PROCESS_VM_READ + QUERY_INFORMATION) within seconds of EID 8.

pivots.label: StartAddress heuristic
pivots.detail: StartAddress in EID 8 pointing to an unbacked memory region (not associated with any loaded module) = shellcode injection. Correlate with Sysmon EID 3 network connection from the target process to a C2 IP within 60 seconds.

hypotheses.fpr: Some AV/EDR products legitimately inject threads into monitored processes. Allowlist known security product executables by signed binary path. Focus alerting on unsigned or user-space source processes injecting into system processes.

hypotheses.title: Process Hollowing via Suspended Process + Unmapping
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of creating a legitimate process in suspended state, unmapping its memory, and replacing it with malicious code before resuming to masquerade as a trusted binary. Hunt for newly created suspended processes quickly followed by WriteProcessMemory and ResumeThread API calls, especially when the process image does not match the on-disk executable.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 + EID 8
pivots.detail: Process created with CREATE_SUSPENDED flag (no direct Sysmon field — infer from: process created AND immediately followed within 100ms by EID 8 CreateRemoteThread from same parent) targeting known hosts like svchost.exe, notepad.exe, explorer.exe.

pivots.label: Image mismatch (EDR)
pivots.detail: EDR telemetry: ProcessImage (from PE header in memory) does not match ProcessPath (on-disk path). This is the definitive indicator of hollow process — requires EDR with memory scanning capability.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 3 anomaly
pivots.detail: svchost.exe or notepad.exe initiating outbound TCP connections to non-Microsoft IPs on unusual ports (4444, 8080, 443 with non-browser UA) is a strong behavioral indicator of a hollowed process executing C2 traffic.

hypotheses.fpr: Application installers and legitimate virtualization software occasionally create suspended processes. Alert only when combined with unusual network behavior from the target process or a parent-child relationship mismatch.

hypotheses.title: DLL Injection via LoadLibrary or Reflective DLL
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of injecting a malicious DLL into a running process by writing its path to remote memory and calling LoadLibraryA/W via CreateRemoteThread, or loading a PE directly from memory via reflective loading. Hunt for Sysmon EID 7 (ImageLoaded) events where a DLL is loaded from a user-writable or temp path into a system process.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 7
pivots.detail: ImageLoaded path matches (%TEMP%\* OR %APPDATA%\* OR C:\Users\*\Downloads\* OR C:\ProgramData\*) AND Image IN (explorer.exe, svchost.exe, notepad.exe, rundll32.exe) AND Signed = false

pivots.label: Reflective DLL marker
pivots.detail: Reflective DLLs load without touching disk — detectable via EDR memory scanning for PE headers in non-module-backed memory regions. Hunt processes with no corresponding ImageLoaded event for memory regions executing code.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 8 + EID 7 chain
pivots.detail: EID 8 CreateRemoteThread into target process within 2 seconds of EID 7 showing unsigned DLL loaded into that same target process = high-confidence injection chain.

refs.label: CISA AA23-193A — Advanced Persistent Threat TTPs

hypotheses.fpr: Some legitimate software loads DLLs from AppData (e.g., browser extensions, plugin frameworks). Focus on system processes loading unsigned DLLs from user-writable paths — this combination has very low FPR.

hypotheses.title: Valid Account Logon from Anomalous Source
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor is suspected of authenticating with a legitimate stolen or compromised credential from an unusual source IP, geography, or at an abnormal time to blend in with normal operations. Hunt for successful logon events (EID 4624) for privileged or service accounts from IPs not in the expected baseline, especially outside business hours or from cloud/VPN exit nodes.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4624
pivots.detail: LogonType IN (2, 3, 10) AND TargetUserName NOT endswith $ AND IpAddress NOT IN (known_office_ranges, VPN_ranges) AND TargetUserName IN (admin accounts, service accounts, IT staff). Time window: 20:00–06:00 local = elevated priority.

pivots.label: Impossible travel
pivots.detail: Same account (TargetUserName) with successful 4624 from two geographically distant IPs within a time window that makes travel physically impossible. Requires GeoIP enrichment on IpAddress field.

pivots.label: New account first use
pivots.detail: TargetUserName last seen >30 days ago suddenly authenticating. Compare 4624 against account last-logon baseline in Active Directory. Reactivated dormant accounts are a strong persistence indicator.

refs.label: CISA AA24-038A — Volt Typhoon valid accounts

hypotheses.fpr: Legitimate remote work, travel, and VPN use generate off-baseline logons. Build a per-account IP/geo/time baseline over 30 days before alerting. Service accounts should never log on interactively — apply stricter thresholds.

hypotheses.title: Service Account Interactive or Network Logon
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor with knowledge of a service account credential is suspected of using it interactively or over the network to move laterally, bypassing human-account monitoring. Hunt for service accounts (accounts with names matching service naming conventions) logging on with LogonType 2 (interactive) or 10 (remote interactive) which are inconsistent with normal service account usage.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4624
pivots.detail: TargetUserName matches (svc_*, *_svc, *service*, *sa_*, *sql*, *iis*, *exchange*) AND LogonType IN (2, 10) — service accounts should only produce LogonType 5 (service). Any interactive logon is anomalous.

pivots.label: 4624 LogonType 3 from unexpected host
pivots.detail: Service account authenticating via network logon (Type 3) from a workstation rather than its designated server. TargetUserName = service account AND WorkstationName NOT IN (expected server list).

pivots.label: 4648 Explicit credential use
pivots.detail: WinEvt 4648 (logon with explicit credentials) where SubjectUserName != TargetUserName and TargetUserName is a service account indicates credential stuffing or pass-the-password of a service credential.

hypotheses.fpr: Some managed service accounts (gMSA) and scheduled tasks produce Type 3 logons from servers. Document expected service account logon patterns per account — alert on any deviation from the documented baseline.

hypotheses.title: RDP Lateral Movement from Non-Admin Workstation
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using RDP to move laterally from a compromised workstation to servers or other workstations, leveraging stolen credentials to expand access. Hunt for EID 4624 LogonType 10 (RemoteInteractive) originating from workstation-class source IPs combined with mstsc.exe process creation on the same source host.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4624 on destination
pivots.detail: LogonType = 10 AND IpAddress matches workstation subnet (not server subnet, not IT admin jump hosts) AND TargetUserName not in (expected RDP users list). Workstation-to-workstation RDP is almost never legitimate.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 on source
pivots.detail: Image = mstsc.exe (RDP client) launched from cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or a non-desktop shortcut parent. mstsc.exe with command-line arguments (/v:target /admin) indicates automated lateral movement.

pivots.label: EID 4778 / 4779
pivots.detail: WinEvt 4778 (session reconnect) or 4779 (session disconnect) from unusual IPs immediately before 4624 Type 10 indicates adversary cycling through RDP sessions across multiple hosts.

refs.label: CISA AA23-075A — LockBit RDP lateral movement

hypotheses.fpr: IT helpdesk and server administrators legitimately use RDP. Allowlist by source IP (jump hosts, IT subnet) and time window (business hours). Alert on workstation-to-workstation RDP and after-hours sessions from non-IT accounts.

hypotheses.title: RDP Enabled on Previously Unexposed Host
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of enabling RDP on a host where it was previously disabled or blocked, creating a persistent remote access channel. Hunt for registry modifications enabling RDP (fDenyTSConnections = 0), firewall rule additions for port 3389, or the first-ever EID 4624 LogonType 10 on a host with no prior RDP history.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 13 registry
pivots.detail: TargetObject = HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\fDenyTSConnections AND Details = DWORD:0 — this key being set to 0 enables RDP. Alert immediately on any modification.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4688 — netsh firewall
pivots.detail: CommandLine contains (netsh advfirewall firewall add rule) AND CommandLine contains (3389 OR RDP OR RemoteDesktop) — adversaries commonly open 3389 via netsh before enabling RDP via registry.

pivots.label: First RDP logon baseline
pivots.detail: Host with no EID 4624 LogonType 10 events in the prior 30 days suddenly receiving a Type 10 logon. Baseline per-host RDP logon history and alert on first occurrence outside a change-management window.

refs.label: CISA AA24-038A — Volt Typhoon RDP enabling

hypotheses.fpr: IT administrators legitimately enable RDP during provisioning. Allowlist changes originating from IT management tools (SCCM, Ansible, DSC). Alert on manual registry edits by interactive user sessions outside change windows.

hypotheses.title: WMI Used to Spawn Process for Lateral Movement or Execution
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of using Windows Management Instrumentation to remotely execute commands or spawn processes on target hosts, bypassing standard remote execution controls. Hunt for processes with a WMI provider host parent (WmiPrvSE.exe) launching shells, scripting engines, or LOLBINs.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — WMI child
pivots.detail: ParentImage endswith WmiPrvSE.exe AND Image IN (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, cscript.exe, wscript.exe, mshta.exe, certutil.exe, bitsadmin.exe, rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe)

pivots.label: WinEvt 4688 — WMI child process
pivots.detail: NewProcessName matches (cmd.exe, powershell.exe) AND ParentProcessName = C:\Windows\System32\wbem\WmiPrvSE.exe. WmiPrvSE spawning shells is almost never legitimate in production.

pivots.label: Network WMI (DCOM)
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 3: DestinationPort = 135 (DCOM endpoint mapper) followed within 10 seconds by EID 1 with WmiPrvSE.exe parent on the target host. Source host is a lateral movement pivot point.

hypotheses.fpr: SCCM, monitoring agents, and some backup solutions use WMI for legitimate management. Allowlist WmiPrvSE.exe child processes spawned under SYSTEM in the context of known management server IPs. Alert on interactive or network-sourced WMI execution.

hypotheses.title: WMI Subscription for Persistence
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of creating a WMI event subscription to achieve fileless persistence that survives reboots and is invisible to most startup auditing tools. Hunt for WMI subscription creation events (EID 5857–5861) or Sysmon events showing creation of ActiveScriptEventConsumer or CommandLineEventConsumer objects.

pivots.label: WinEvt 5861 — subscription creation
pivots.detail: EventID 5861 in Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational log indicates a new permanent WMI event subscription. Any new subscription outside a documented management baseline warrants investigation.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 19/20/21
pivots.detail: EID 19 = WmiEventFilter created, EID 20 = WmiEventConsumer created, EID 21 = WmiEventConsumerToFilter binding. All three within seconds of each other = complete persistence subscription installed. CommandLineEventConsumer CommandLineTemplate containing cmd.exe or powershell.exe = immediate escalation.

pivots.label: MOF file drop
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 11 showing .mof file creation in C:\Windows\System32\wbem\ by a non-SYSTEM process, followed by mofcomp.exe execution — adversaries compile malicious MOF files to register WMI subscriptions.

hypotheses.fpr: Some endpoint management and monitoring products (SCCM, WMI-based inventory) create WMI subscriptions legitimately. Maintain a whitelist of known subscription names; alert on any subscription with a CommandLineTemplate or ScriptText that executes shells.

hypotheses.title: Scheduled Task Creation via schtasks.exe with Suspicious Action
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of creating a scheduled task via schtasks.exe to achieve persistence or delayed execution of a payload, often combining it with LOLBINs or encoded commands to evade detection. Hunt for schtasks.exe /create with actions pointing to scripting engines, LOLBINs, or temp paths.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — schtasks create
pivots.detail: Image = schtasks.exe AND CommandLine contains /create AND CommandLine contains (/tr OR /xml) AND CommandLine contains (cmd.exe OR powershell.exe OR wscript.exe OR cscript.exe OR mshta.exe OR rundll32.exe OR regsvr32.exe OR %TEMP% OR %APPDATA%)

pivots.label: Task XML drop + import
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 11: .xml file created in %TEMP% or user-writable path, followed within 10 seconds by schtasks.exe /create /xml pointing to that file. This pattern evades CommandLine detection of the action payload.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — task-spawned child
pivots.detail: ParentImage = C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe (task host) AND ParentCommandLine contains taskeng.exe OR taskhostw.exe, and child Image = powershell.exe or cmd.exe with encoded or obfuscated arguments.

hypotheses.fpr: Software installers and IT management tools create scheduled tasks extensively. Focus alerting on tasks created by user-context processes (not SYSTEM/LocalService), tasks with actions in temp/AppData paths, and tasks with encoded PowerShell actions.

hypotheses.title: Scheduled Task Modification of Existing System Task
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of hijacking an existing legitimate scheduled task by modifying its action to execute a malicious payload, maintaining the appearance of a known-good task name to evade detection. Hunt for modifications to pre-existing task XML files in C:\Windows\System32\Tasks or registry-based task entries.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 11 — task folder write
pivots.detail: TargetFilename starts with C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\ AND Image NOT IN (svchost.exe, taskeng.exe, taskhostw.exe) AND NOT (Image endswith MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe OR GoogleUpdate.exe) — direct task XML write by a non-system process is highly suspicious.

pivots.label: WinEvt 4698 + 4702
pivots.detail: EID 4698 (task created) or 4702 (task modified) in Security log. TaskName matching an existing Windows task name with a modified action is a hijack indicator. Correlate SubjectUserName with expected admin accounts.

pivots.label: Registry task modification
pivots.detail: Sysmon EID 13: TargetObject starts with HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\TaskCache\Tasks AND Details contains (cmd.exe OR powershell.exe OR %TEMP%) — some persistence frameworks write tasks directly to registry.

hypotheses.fpr: Windows Update, software updaters (Chrome, Edge, Adobe), and endpoint management solutions modify scheduled tasks regularly. Maintain a baseline of known-good task names and their expected action executables; alert on any deviation.

hypotheses.title: Registry Run Key Persistence Added by Unsigned Process
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of adding a registry Run or RunOnce key to achieve user-level persistence that executes a payload at logon. Hunt for Sysmon EID 13 registry modifications targeting HKCU or HKLM Run keys by processes that are unsigned, executing from temp paths, or spawned by Office applications or scripting engines.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 13 — Run key add
pivots.detail: TargetObject matches (HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\* OR HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\* OR HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce\*) AND Image NOT IN (known installers, SYSTEM processes, msiexec.exe)

pivots.label: Payload path in value
pivots.detail: Details (registry value data) contains (%TEMP%\* OR %APPDATA%\* OR C:\Users\*\Downloads\* OR C:\ProgramData\*) AND value data NOT signed. Persistence pointing to temp paths is a near-certain indicator of malware.

pivots.label: Suspicious parent chain
pivots.detail: Image of process writing Run key has parent chain: Office app (winword.exe, excel.exe) → cmd.exe/wscript.exe → registry write. This chain = document macro dropping persistence payload.

hypotheses.fpr: Software installers legitimately add Run keys. Allowlist by: signed installer process (msiexec, vendor-signed setup.exe) and known software paths (C:\Program Files\*). Alert specifically on unsigned processes or payload paths in user-writable directories.

hypotheses.title: Security-Relevant Registry Key Tampered to Disable Defenses
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of modifying security-relevant registry keys to disable Windows Defender, disable UAC, or alter audit policy to reduce detection visibility. Hunt for Sysmon EID 13 or WinEvt 4657 events targeting known defense-impacting registry paths by non-SYSTEM processes.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 13 — Defender disable
pivots.detail: TargetObject matches (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\DisableAntiSpyware OR HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Real-Time Protection\DisableRealtimeMonitoring) AND Details = DWORD:1

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 13 — UAC bypass
pivots.detail: TargetObject = HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\EnableLUA AND Details = DWORD:0. Disabling UAC removes one of the most effective privilege barriers and should never occur outside imaging workflows.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 13 — audit policy
pivots.detail: TargetObject matches HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Mini\Audit\* — adversaries disable ETW or security audit logging here to blind SIEM collection before staging further actions.

hypotheses.fpr: Enterprise AV management consoles and GPO templates can write Defender policy keys legitimately. Allowlist writes originating from SYSTEM or known management agent processes. Manual interactive modification of these keys outside change windows = near-zero FPR.

hypotheses.title: Windows Defender Tampered via Set-MpPreference or sc stop
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of disabling or degrading Windows Defender using Set-MpPreference, sc.exe stop, or net.exe stop commands to remove the primary host-based detection layer before deploying ransomware or a persistent implant. Hunt for these commands in process creation or ScriptBlock logs, especially when executed from unusual parent processes.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — PowerShell
pivots.detail: Image = powershell.exe AND CommandLine contains (Set-MpPreference AND (-Disable OR -Exclusion OR -SubmitSamplesConsent 0 OR -SignatureDisableUpdateOnStartupWithoutEngine))

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — sc/net stop
pivots.detail: Image IN (sc.exe, net.exe, net1.exe) AND CommandLine matches (stop.*WinDefend OR stop.*MsMpSvc OR stop.*SecurityHealthService OR stop.*WdNisSvc). Also: taskkill.exe /F /IM MsMpEng.exe

pivots.label: PS EID 4104 — ScriptBlock
pivots.detail: ScriptBlockText contains (Set-MpPreference OR Add-MpPreference) AND ScriptBlockText contains (-Disable OR ExclusionPath OR ExclusionProcess). Ransomware groups commonly exclude their staging directory before detonating the encryptor.

hypotheses.fpr: Penetration testers and security assessment tools may disable Defender in approved test environments. In production, any Defender disablement outside an authorized change window with documented approval warrants immediate escalation. FPR is near-zero in hardened environments.

hypotheses.title: EDR Process or Driver Killed via BYOVD or Process Termination
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor on Windows is suspected of terminating EDR agent processes or unloading their kernel drivers using a Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) technique or direct process termination to blind the endpoint before deploying a payload. Hunt for vulnerable driver loads followed by sudden termination of security product processes.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 6 — vulnerable driver load
pivots.detail: ImageLoaded path matches known BYOVD-abused drivers (gdrv.sys, RTCore64.sys, zamguard64.sys, iqvw64e.sys, mhyprot2.sys) OR Sysmon EID 7 with unsigned driver loaded from %TEMP% or user-writable path.

pivots.label: Sysmon EID 1 — security process kill
pivots.detail: Image IN (taskkill.exe, tskill.exe) AND CommandLine contains (MsMpEng.exe OR SentinelAgent.exe OR CylanceSvc.exe OR cb.exe OR CSFalconService.exe OR bdagent.exe OR kavtsd.exe). Any attempt to kill a known AV/EDR process by name.

pivots.label: WinEvt 7036 — service stopped
pivots.detail: ServiceName IN (WinDefend, SentinelAgent, CrowdStrike Falcon Sensor, CarbonBlack, Cylance) AND ServiceState = stopped. Security service stopping outside a planned maintenance window = immediate escalation.

hypotheses.fpr: EDR/AV processes may restart themselves after updates, appearing as a stop/start cycle. Allowlist service restarts triggered by the security vendor's own update service. Alert on terminations initiated by non-vendor processes or by drivers loaded from non-standard paths.
